Membership is the job

By lowob · 17 July 2026 · 6-minute read · Growth

A media audience is a list until it is a membership; build the membership on sourcing, amplification and peer value, then measure it like a business line.

The number that is not a community

Media founders report audience numbers because they are easy to count. Subscribers, followers, opens, downloads. None of these are a community. A community is a set of people with a relationship to you and to each other.

Part 26 made the point that an audience is not a business. The same logic applies here. An audience is not a community either. It is the pool you recruit a community from.

Part 5 defined community as a job with an owner, a budget and a measure. In media the job is membership. The output is people who pay, show up, contribute and refer. That is the whole definition. If a person does none of those four things, they are a reader, not a member.

The three contributions that matter

Members do a lot of things. Three of them change the business.

Sourcing. Members send tips, data, documents and questions. The best stories in niche media come from the people closest to the subject. A member who sends one good lead a quarter is worth more than a thousand passive subscribers. Make it easy: a standing inbox, a members' thread, an editor who replies within a day.

Amplification, but the right kind. You do not need members who post your work to the public. You need members who forward it to the three peers who matter. Niche media grows through private channels: a message to a colleague, a mention in a team meeting. Ask for that explicitly. "Who on your team should see this?" beats "please share."

Peer value. This is the one that holds. Members who want access to each other will stay through a bad month of content. A platform can copy your format and outbid you for writers. It cannot copy a room of people who already trust each other. Everything in the design below serves this.

Designing the membership

Four decisions, made deliberately.

What is behind the wall. Not everything. Put the things that depend on trust behind it: data, source documents, the editor's working notes, the questions members ask each other. Keep the public layer strong enough to recruit from.

Rituals. A ritual is a fixed time when members expect each other. A weekly call with a set agenda. A members' thread that opens every Monday with one question. An annual gathering, even if it is twenty people in a borrowed room. Rituals are the mechanism for peer value. Without them, the wall is just a paywall.

Recognition. Name contributors in the work. Give members access to the editor that readers do not get. Recognition costs attention, not money, and it is the cheapest retention tool you have.

A members' council. Six to ten members, rotating, who meet quarterly. They tell you what the membership wants and when you have drifted. They also become your first recruiters, because the role gives them something to say about you.

The first hundred for media

Part 6 argued that the first hundred people set the shape of everything after. For media, the test is simple. The first hundred members are the hundred readers whose job titles you would put in the sponsor deck.

That means recruiting by name, not by funnel. List the hundred. Write to each one. Tell them what the membership is for and why they specifically are on the list. Expect to do this yourself, because nobody else can.

The composition of the first hundred becomes your pitch to sponsors later on. It also becomes the peer value for the next hundred. Get the roles right before you get the number up.

Owned channels only

Members live on channels you control. Email, and a members' space on a platform where you hold the export and the relationship. Part 26 covered owned versus rented. For membership the rule is stricter: if the platform can change the terms, it cannot hold the membership.

A social platform group is fine for recruiting. It is not where the membership lives. The moment you depend on a feed to reach your own members, you have handed the job to someone who does not have it.

What to measure

Four numbers, reported monthly, replacing the audience numbers you report now.

Measure What it tells you
Member retention Whether the wall and the rituals are worth paying for
Contribution rate Share of members who sourced, posted or asked in the period
Member referrals New members who were introduced by an existing one
Paid revenue from referring members Whether peer value is funding the business

The last one matters most. If a growing share of paid revenue comes from members who brought someone, the membership is working. If it stays flat while the list grows, you have a newsletter with a paywall. Part 9 covers why reach reporting hides this.

The checklist

Membership has an owner, a budget line and a monthly report.

The three contributions are asked for explicitly: sourcing, peer amplification, peer value.

One ritual on the calendar that members attend for each other.

Contributors named in the work; members' council meeting quarterly.

First hundred listed by name and job title, recruited personally.

Members held on email and a space you can export; retention, contribution and referral tracked.

lowob takeaways

  • Subscribers, followers, opens and downloads are not a community; they are the pool a community is recruited from.
  • Rituals, such as a weekly call or a Monday members' thread, are the mechanism for peer value.
  • Track member retention, contribution rate, member referrals, and paid revenue from referring members.
